rv.q: The most fun you can have on Broadway right now, A Gentleman’s Guide to Love and Murder is, in a word, peerless.
A daffy, inspired musical with brilliant performance that deserves to be immortalized in Broadway lore.
The hilarious satire on Edwardian melodrama, featuring the incomparable and seemingly tireless Jefferson Mays in eight roles.
Although the naughty lyrics are the sweetest of the show’s bitter treats, Steven Lutvak’s music invites its own independent smiles.
In an increasingly risk-averse Broadway landscape where more and more musicals come from mainstream-brand movies or hit song catalogues, this bright little jewel is a legitimate treat.
Missing, alas, is a courageous editor.
Too bad the show doesn’t spend even more time getting away from murder — love becomes it so much more.

In “Gentleman’s Guide,” which opened Sunday at the Theatre, the coveted title has been changed to the Earl of Highhurst, and that is perhaps the least of the improvements made in this brilliant transfer to the musical stage.
Quite simply, it's a bloody good time.
This is Mays' show — and he seems to have as grand a time carrying it as you will watching him.
It's fresh, and it's tremendously entertaining.
A Gentleman's Guide to Love and Murder is a deliriously entertaining musical comedy that manages to be both sophisticated and silly, murderous and musical.
It's tough to remember another Broadway outing that's derived so much gleeful entertainment.

A stylish music-hall mystery in which we know whodunit from beginning to end, A Gentleman's Guide to Love and Murder has lively songs, a congenial villain and a physically and morally flexible mistress
Everything about the show is so likable.
Yet for all its cleverness and wicked charm, this is an entertainment I could easily have skipped.
There's not one number that really stands out and at times the music actually slows down the action.
With a thin premise, a sluggish book and unmemorable songs that vaguely resemble work by Gilbert & Sullivan and Noel Coward, the show makes for a tiresome 21/2 hours.
Gentleman's Guide is a pocket-sized musical that dazzles with lyrical wit, dark comedic fun and bravura showmanship.

It sets out to be a confection of light entertainment and achieves that goal in every way possible. Mind you, this is not my cuppa tea in general, but that is not the point. The point is that all the parts come together exactly as they were meant to, and thus we have a cube of sugar that is exquisite.
Pinkham manages the difficult task of making us care about a serial killer and Mays is simply amazing.
A Gentlemen’s Guide ranks as one of the highlights of the fall season.
The only danger you’ll be in for is having too good a time.
